[1] Global Layout and Structure:
The diagram is vertically structured into two parallel workflows side-by-side, each starting from an input image at the top. Both workflows consist of sequential processing stages represented as rounded rectangular modules connected by downward-pointing arrows. The left pipeline represents the traditional method, while the right pipeline shows the proposed end-to-end model. Below these two pipelines, a confusion matrix is displayed, summarizing classification performance across eight room categories.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes:
Each pipeline begins with an identical input image depicting an indoor scene. In the left pipeline, the first module is labeled 'Multiscale patches extractor' and contains a visual representation of multiple cropped image patches of varying sizes. This is followed by a 'CNN features extractor' module, shown as six vertical bars with distinct color gradients (green, red, blue, yellow, purple, gray), symbolizing extracted feature vectors. The final module is an 'NBNN-based classifier', depicted as an orange rounded rectangle containing a circular diagram with five colored dots (red, yellow, green) and a central question mark, representing the classification decision process.

In the right pipeline, the first module is 'Scaling', illustrated with a dashed-line bounding box overlaying the input image, indicating spatial resizing or normalization. This feeds into the 'Fully Convolutional CNN-NBNN' module, also shown as an orange rounded rectangle, which combines both feature extraction and classification. It includes the same six color-gradient bars as the left pipeline’s feature extractor, followed by the identical circular classifier diagram with colored dots and a question mark.

The orange color of the 'NBNN-based classifier' and 'Fully Convolutional CNN-NBNN' modules visually indicates that these components involve a learning phase, as noted in the caption. All other modules are gray.

[3] Connections and Arrows:
Downward-pointing arrows connect the modules within each pipeline, indicating the flow of data. From the input image, an arrow leads to the 'Multiscale patches extractor' in the left pipeline and to 'Scaling' in the right pipeline. Subsequent arrows connect each module sequentially: from patch extractor to CNN features extractor, then to the NBNN-based classifier in the left; from scaling to Fully Convolutional CNN-NBNN in the right. No cross-pipeline connections exist.

At the bottom, the confusion matrix displays classification results for eight room types: bathroom, bedroom, children room, closet, corridor, dining room, kitchen, and living room. Rows represent ground truth labels, columns represent predicted labels. Diagonal cells (correct classifications) are highlighted in dark gray or black, with numbers indicating counts. Off-diagonal cells show misclassifications, with lighter shading for smaller errors. For example, 17 bathroom images were correctly classified, while 1 bedroom image was misclassified as bathroom. The matrix provides quantitative validation of the proposed model’s accuracy.

The figure illustrates the core architecture of a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), depicting the adversarial interaction between two neural network components: the Generator and the Discriminator. The global layout is horizontal and left-to-right, structured as a workflow diagram with distinct functional modules connected by arrows indicating data flow and processing direction.

On the far left, a latent variable denoted as 'z' is represented as a black-bordered rounded rectangle with bold black text. This serves as the random input vector for the Generator. An arrow in solid green connects 'z' to the Generator module, which is depicted as a larger rounded rectangle with a light green border and bold black text labeled 'Generator'.

The Generator outputs generated fake data, labeled 'X_fake', shown as a black-bordered rounded rectangle with bold black text beneath which the phrase 'Generated fake data' appears in smaller black font. A solid green arrow connects the Generator to this output box.

To the right of the Generator’s output, real data is introduced as another black-bordered rounded rectangle labeled 'X_real', positioned above 'X_fake' and accompanied by the label 'Real data' in bold black text above it. Both 'X_real' and 'X_fake' feed into the Discriminator module via dashed blue arrows, indicating that both real and generated data are inputs to the Discriminator.

The Discriminator is represented as a large rounded rectangle with a blue border and bold black text labeled 'Discriminator'. It receives both real and fake data streams and processes them to determine authenticity.

Finally, an arrow in solid blue extends from the Discriminator to a traffic-light-style icon on the far right, consisting of two vertically stacked circles — green on top and red below — enclosed in a blue border. Above this icon, the label 'Distinguishing real or fake' is written in bold black text, indicating the Discriminator’s binary classification task: assigning real (green) or fake (red) labels to incoming data samples.

All text elements are in black, sans-serif font, with module names in bold. The color coding is consistent: green for Generator-related components and flows, blue for Discriminator-related components and flows, and black for data representations and labels. The diagram uses rounded rectangles for all functional blocks and circles for the output indicator. The connections are clearly differentiated: solid arrows for direct data generation and processing, and dashed arrows for input feeding into the Discriminator from both real and fake sources.

The figure presents a Synchronous Data Flow Graph (SDFG) representation of a JPEG Encoder, enclosed within a dashed rectangular boundary labeled 'JPEG Encoder' at the top right. The global layout is linear and left-to-right, depicting a sequence of processing stages connected by directed edges indicating data flow. The graph consists of five main nodes, each representing a computational module, with associated data rates and connections.

Starting from the left, the first node is an orange circle labeled 'get_MB', positioned below which is the text 'get_MB'. This node receives input from three external sources indicated by dashed lines: 'Actor', 'Rate', and 'Delay', all written in blue text above the node. From 'get_MB', a solid arrow points to the next stage, marked with the number '768' above the arrow, indicating the data rate. The second node is a small black dot labeled '2D' beneath it, with two such dots shown side-by-side, suggesting a dual or parallel processing step. An arrow from this node to the next is labeled '128' above it.

The third node is a green circle labeled 'CC' below it, representing the color conversion stage. A solid arrow from 'CC' to the next node is labeled '64' above it. The fourth node is a light blue circle labeled 'DCT' below it, denoting the Discrete Cosine Transform stage. Another solid arrow labeled '64' connects 'DCT' to the final node. The fifth and last node is a dark blue circle labeled 'VLC' below it, representing Variable Length Coding. The arrow leading into 'VLC' is also labeled '64'.

Additionally, a dashed line from the label 'Channel' in blue text above the graph points to the edge between 'CC' and 'DCT', indicating that this segment of the pipeline is subject to channel constraints or modeling. All arrows are solid except for the dashed lines from external inputs ('Actor', 'Rate', 'Delay') and the 'Channel' annotation. The entire diagram uses a light beige background, and all node labels and annotations are in black or blue text, with numerical data rates placed above the connecting arrows. The structure reflects a typical JPEG encoding pipeline with explicit data rate annotations for each stage transition.

The figure illustrates the architecture of the SuperPoint decoders, which consist of two parallel branches: the Interest Point Decoder and the Descriptor Decoder. The global layout is left-to-right, starting with an input image of size W×H×1, which is processed by an Encoder block. The Encoder is represented as a dashed rectangular box containing four progressively smaller gray 3D blocks, indicating a series of convolutional layers that downsample the input spatially. The output of the Encoder is a feature map of size W/8 × H/8, which serves as the shared input for both decoders.

The Interest Point Decoder is enclosed in a dashed box at the top. It begins with a Conv layer, shown as a gray 3D block, producing a feature map of size W/8 × H/8 × 65. This is followed by a Softmax operation, depicted as a blue rectangle, which normalizes the output across the 65 channels. The result is then passed through a Reshape operation, also shown as a blue rectangle, to convert the feature map into a 2D probability map of size W × H × 1, representing the confidence scores for interest points at each pixel location. A diagonal arrow labeled 'χ' connects the 65-channel feature map to the Softmax, indicating the channel-wise processing.

Below it, the Descriptor Decoder is similarly enclosed in a dashed box. It starts with a Conv layer, again shown as a gray 3D block, generating a feature map of size W/8 × H/8 × D, where D denotes the descriptor dimension. This is followed by a Bi-Cubic Interpolate operation, shown as a blue rectangle, which upsamples the feature map back to the original spatial resolution W × H. The output is then normalized using L2 Norm, another blue rectangle, to produce a final descriptor map of size W × H × D. A diagonal arrow labeled 'D' connects the D-channel feature map to the interpolation step, indicating the channel dimension being processed.

Both decoders share the same input from the Encoder and use non-learned upsampling (Bi-Cubic Interpolation) to restore spatial resolution, as noted in the caption. The outputs are visualized as 3D blocks on the far right: the Interest Point Decoder outputs a single-channel map (W×H×1), while the Descriptor Decoder outputs a D-channel map (W×H×D). All connections between modules are indicated by solid black arrows, showing the forward flow of data. The figure uses consistent visual attributes: gray 3D blocks for convolutional layers, blue rectangles for operations like Softmax, Reshape, Bi-Cubic Interpolate, and L2 Norm, and dashed boxes to group related components into functional units.

The figure illustrates the conceptual framework of ILRMA (Independent Low-Rank Matrix Analysis), a method for blind source separation in the time-frequency domain. The global layout is left-to-right, depicting a signal processing pipeline starting from observed signals, passing through a demixing stage, and culminating in low-rank approximation for source estimation.

On the far left, two purple waveform traces labeled 'Observed signal' represent mixed audio inputs. These signals feed into a rectangular gray box labeled 'Frequency-wise demixing matrix', which processes them independently across frequency bins. From this module, two output waveforms emerge: a red waveform and a blue waveform, labeled collectively as 'Estimated signal'. These represent the separated sources after demixing.

A dashed feedback loop connects the estimated signals back to the demixing matrix, accompanied by the text: 'Update demixing matrix so that estimated signals are mutually independent and have low-rank structure in time-frequency domain'. This indicates an iterative optimization process where the demixing matrix is adjusted to enforce both statistical independence and low-rank structure in the time-frequency representation of the estimated sources.

To the right, within a dashed rectangular boundary labeled 'Low-rank approximation', two time-frequency spectrograms are shown. Each is a grid with axes labeled 'Frequency' (vertical) and 'Time' (horizontal). The grids consist of black and white squares, representing varying energy levels or activation patterns. The top spectrogram is labeled T₁V₁, and the bottom one T₂V₂, indicating that each estimated signal is modeled as a product of a time component (T) and a frequency component (V), forming a low-rank matrix decomposition. Thick black arrows point from the estimated signals to these spectrograms, signifying that the time-frequency representations are derived from the estimated signals and then decomposed into low-rank structures.

The visual modules include rectangular boxes for processing stages, waveform plots for signals, and grid-based spectrograms for time-frequency representations. Colors are used to distinguish signals: purple for observed, red and blue for estimated. Text labels are clear and positioned near relevant components. The overall structure emphasizes the iterative nature of the algorithm, combining independence maximization with low-rank modeling in the time-frequency domain.

The figure illustrates the AOD-Net architecture for single image dehazing, which serves as inspiration for EVD-Net. The overall layout is a left-to-right flowchart depicting a deep neural network pipeline from input to output. The structure consists of two main functional modules: the K-estimation Module and the Clean Image Generation Module, connected sequentially.

The K-estimation Module occupies the central portion of the diagram and comprises five layers (Layer1 to Layer5), each containing one or more convolutional or concatenation operations. The module begins with an input tensor represented as a yellow rectangular prism. This input flows into a sequence of processing blocks: Conv1 (blue rectangular prism), Conv2 (blue), Concat1 (green), Conv3 (blue), Concat2 (green), Conv4 (blue), Concat3 (green), and finally conv5(K) (blue). These blocks are arranged horizontally in order, forming a feed-forward path. Above each block, dashed blue arrows point downward from labels 'Layer1' through 'Layer5', indicating the hierarchical layering of the network. Additionally, skip connections are shown via dashed blue lines connecting earlier layers to later concatenation blocks: Layer1 connects to Concat1, Layer2 to Concat2, and Layer3 to Concat3, enabling feature reuse across layers. The entire K-estimation Module is labeled at the bottom with a blue underline.

Following the K-estimation Module, a dashed blue arrow leads to the Clean Image Generation Module, depicted as a rounded rectangle with a blue border. Inside this box is the mathematical formula J(x) = K(x)I(x) - K(x), representing the dehazing equation where I(x) is the input hazy image and K(x) is the estimated transmission map. Below the formula, the module is explicitly labeled 'Clean Image Generation Module'.

A final dashed blue arrow extends from this module to the output, represented by another yellow rectangular prism identical in shape and color to the input, signifying the restored clean image. The entire diagram uses consistent visual attributes: blue prisms for convolutional layers, green prisms for concatenation layers, and yellow prisms for input/output. All connections are dashed blue arrows, indicating data flow. The figure is captioned as 'The AOD-Net architecture for single image dehazing \cite{ICCV17a,li2017all}, which inspires EVD-Net.'

The figure illustrates the architectural flow of a variational autoencoder (VAE), presented as a left-to-right sequential pipeline. The global layout consists of six main components arranged horizontally: an input vector X, an Encoder module, two output parameters from the encoder (μ and σ), a latent variable z, a Decoder module, and the reconstructed output Y. All components are represented as rectangular blocks with black borders, except for the latent variable z, which is light blue, while the input X and output Y are green, and the mean μ and standard deviation σ are yellow. The Encoder and Decoder are large gray rectangles labeled accordingly, indicating they are multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). The input X, a tall green rectangle labeled 'X', feeds into the Encoder via a thick black arrow pointing right. From the Encoder, two separate thick black arrows branch out diagonally upward and downward to two vertically aligned yellow rectangles labeled 'μ' (mean) and 'σ' (standard deviation), respectively. These two parameters are then combined to form the latent variable z through a convergence point: two thick black arrows point from μ and σ toward a central light blue rectangle labeled 'z'. This represents the reparameterization trick, where z = μ + σ ⊙ ε, though the epsilon term is not visually depicted. A single thick black arrow extends from z to the Decoder, another large gray rectangle labeled 'Decoder'. Finally, a thick black arrow leads from the Decoder to the output Y, a tall green rectangle labeled 'Y', representing the reconstructed data. The diagram emphasizes the probabilistic nature of the latent space by explicitly showing the derivation of z from μ and σ, and the overall structure reflects the VAE’s generative process: encoding input into a distribution over latent variables, sampling from that distribution, and decoding back to reconstruct the input.

The figure illustrates the ODC (Overlapping Domain Cover) framework, a multi-stage machine learning methodology designed for data partitioning and local model training. The global layout is a horizontal workflow diagram composed of five main stages connected by light green rightward arrows, indicating sequential progression from left to right. The first stage on the far left shows a scattered set of yellow circular data points, representing raw input data. This is followed by a sequence of four rectangular processing blocks, each with a light blue gradient fill and black border, labeled sequentially: 'Equal Size Clustering', 'Overlapping Domain Cover Generation', 'Training local Models', and 'Prediction/Test'.

In the second stage, 'Equal Size Clustering', the raw data points are grouped into clusters of equal size, though this step is not visually depicted beyond the initial data scatter. The third stage, 'Overlapping Domain Cover Generation', is visually represented by a cluster of overlapping circles in multiple colors—red, blue, green, orange, and black—each enclosing some of the yellow data points. These circles symbolize overlapping domains or regions covering the data space, with significant overlap between them, indicating that data points may belong to multiple domains simultaneously.

The fourth stage, 'Training local Models', is shown with the same overlapping circle structure, but now each circle is annotated with a mathematical function label such as f₁(x*), f₂(x*), ..., f₆(x*), indicating that a local model is trained within each domain. The functions are written in black text inside the respective colored circles, and the notation x* suggests that these models are trained using specific data points or representations within each domain. The final stage, 'Prediction/Test', is a simple block indicating the application of the trained local models for prediction or testing purposes.

Connections between stages are represented by thick, light green arrows pointing right, emphasizing the forward flow of the pipeline. The visual modules are consistent in style: all processing blocks are rounded rectangles with a glossy blue gradient, while the data points are small yellow circles with subtle shadows. The overlapping circles in the middle stages are distinct in color and size, with clear boundaries and transparent fills to show overlaps. The entire diagram is clean, schematic, and emphasizes the modular and sequential nature of the ODC framework, from clustering to local model training and final prediction.

The figure presents a schematic overview of a natural language to SQL query generation system, structured as a left-to-right dataflow pipeline with feedback loops. The global layout is horizontal, starting from user input on the far left and progressing through processing modules toward SQL output on the right, with an iterative refinement loop between two central components.

On the far left, a human user icon (depicted as a person in a suit with a speech bubble) provides a natural language query: 'List total annual income of tax payers...'. This input flows via a black arrow into a blue-bordered rounded rectangle labeled 'Semantic parser', which processes the natural language to extract meaning. Simultaneously, a database icon (a stack of three blue disks) feeds into another blue-bordered rounded rectangle labeled 'Database Analysis', which extracts schema information and statistics from the database.

The outputs from both the Semantic parser and Database Analysis converge into a green-bordered rounded rectangle labeled 'Program synthesis'. The Semantic parser sends a 'Query sketch' to this module, while the Database Analysis sends 'Schema+stats'. The Program synthesis module attempts to generate a valid SQL query based on these inputs. A black arrow with a green checkmark points upward from this module to a window icon labeled 'SQL', which displays a sample generated query: 'SELECT F.Year ... FROM TAX_PAYER ... WHERE F.Year > 1986'.

If the generated query is invalid or incorrect, a red 'X' symbol appears above a bidirectional curved arrow connecting the Program synthesis module to a red-bordered rounded rectangle labeled 'Sketch repair'. This indicates a feedback loop: the failed attempt triggers the Sketch repair module, which produces a 'New sketch' (labeled along the return arrow) that is sent back to the Program synthesis module for reprocessing. This iterative process continues until a correct SQL query is synthesized.

All modules are represented as rounded rectangles with distinct border colors: blue for input processing stages (Semantic parser, Database Analysis), green for the core synthesis engine (Program synthesis), and red for the error correction stage (Sketch repair). Text labels for data flows ('Query sketch', 'Schema+stats', 'New sketch') are placed along the respective arrows. The figure uses simple icons (user, database, SQL window) to represent external entities, and employs visual cues like checkmarks and crosses to indicate success or failure in the query generation process.

The figure presents an overview of a self-reinforced cascaded regression framework, structured as a closed-loop iterative process involving three main components: label prediction (S), survival (v), and regression weights (W). The global layout is a top-down flowchart with a feedback loop connecting the bottom modules back to the top, forming a cyclic update mechanism. At the top left, a rectangular box labeled 'Initialize S_{t+1} v_{t+1}' serves as the starting point, indicating the initialization of the label prediction and survival variables for the next iteration. A thick blue arrow points from this box to the central top box, labeled 'Update W_{t+1}', which contains the optimization objective: min(∑_{s_i ∈ S} R(s_i, f_i, w)) + μΩ(w). This represents the minimization of a loss function combining reconstruction error R and a regularization term Ω, weighted by hyperparameter μ. From this central box, a rightward then downward L-shaped blue arrow leads to the bottom-right module, 'Update S_{t+1}', which visually demonstrates the refinement of facial landmark positions. It shows a face image on the left, with a corresponding image on the right where numerous blue dots mark facial landmarks, indicating the updated label prediction. A blue arrow points from this module to the bottom-left module, 'Update v_{t+1}', which illustrates the survival variable update through two visual examples. On the left, under 'Local appearance discrepancy', two close-up face regions show red and blue dots with dashed circles, suggesting local feature matching or error assessment. On the right, under 'Global geometry discrepancy', two full-face images display white lines connecting blue dots, representing geometric alignment or structural consistency. A blue arrow from this module loops back to the 'Update W_{t+1}' box, completing the closed-loop structure. All boxes have blue borders, and the arrows are thick and blue, emphasizing the flow direction. The figure uses real face images to ground the abstract updates in visual context, with text labels clearly identifying each stage and its purpose.

The figure presents an architectural overview of ResRNN, a dual-path deep learning framework designed for estimating Relative Wall Thickness (RWT) from cardiac image sequences. The layout is horizontally oriented and divided into two parallel pathways enclosed within dashed blue rectangular boundaries: the upper 'RNN path: Residual Estimation' and the lower 'CNN path: Preliminary Estimation'. Both paths receive identical input images, depicted as grayscale cardiac cross-sections on the far left of each path.

In the CNN path (lower), the input image is processed by a light blue rectangular module labeled 'CNN Embedding', which extracts feature representations. These features are then passed to a dark gray rectangular module labeled 'Fully-connected (fc) layer', which generates a preliminary RWT estimation. This path serves as a baseline estimation component.

In the RNN path (upper), the same input image is also fed into a light blue 'CNN Embedding' module, identical in appearance and function to the one in the lower path. The output of this module is then sequentially processed by two dark gray rectangular modules: first, 'Temporal RNN', which captures temporal dynamics across the sequence, followed by 'Spatial RNN', which models spatial relationships within each frame. This path is responsible for estimating the residual error relative to the preliminary estimation.

A bidirectional yellow arrow labeled 'shared' connects the two 'CNN Embedding' modules, indicating that they share the same weights and parameters, ensuring consistent feature extraction across both paths.

The outputs from both paths converge at a yellow plus sign symbol, representing element-wise addition. The result of this summation is directed to an orange rectangular box labeled 'RWT Estimation', which represents the final predicted RWT value. Solid black arrows indicate the forward data flow throughout the network, while the shared connection is highlighted with a distinct yellow bidirectional arrow to emphasize parameter sharing. The overall structure reflects a residual learning strategy where the CNN path provides an initial prediction and the RNN path refines it by estimating and adding the residual error.

The figure illustrates an encoder-decoder neural network architecture designed for image segmentation, likely applied to medical or industrial imaging data, as suggested by the input images showing a cross-sectional view of a mechanical component and a grayscale scan. The global layout is linear and left-to-right, depicting a forward pass through the network from input to output. On the far left, two input images are shown: a binary mask (black and white) and a grayscale image, both representing the same object, which are fed into the network via a large blue arrow. The core of the architecture consists of a sequence of 3D rectangular blocks arranged horizontally, symbolizing layers in the network. These blocks are color-coded and labeled according to their function, as explained in the legend at the bottom: blue blocks represent 'Conv + ReLU' (convolutional layer followed by ReLU activation), light blue blocks denote 'Dropout', orange blocks indicate 'Pooling', green blocks signify 'Upsampling', and yellow blocks represent 'Conv + Sigmoid'.

The network begins with a blue block labeled '16', indicating 16 feature maps, followed by an orange 'Pooling' block, then a series of blue 'Conv + ReLU' blocks with labels '32' and '32', suggesting two layers producing 32 feature maps each. This is followed by another orange 'Pooling' block, then four consecutive blue 'Conv + ReLU' blocks labeled '64', indicating 64 feature maps. The decoder path starts with a green 'Upsampling' block, which increases spatial resolution, followed by a blue 'Conv + ReLU' block labeled '32', then a light blue 'Dropout' block, another blue 'Conv + ReLU' block labeled '32', and a second green 'Upsampling' block. The final stages consist of a blue 'Conv + ReLU' block labeled '16', and a yellow 'Conv + Sigmoid' block labeled '1', which outputs a single-channel segmentation map. Two skip connections are depicted as dashed blue lines with arrows: one connects the first '32' block in the encoder to the corresponding position after the first upsampling in the decoder, and the second connects the second '32' block in the encoder to the position after the second upsampling in the decoder. These skip connections concatenate feature maps from earlier encoder layers to later decoder layers, preserving spatial information. The output of the network is shown on the far right as a black-and-white segmented image, matching the shape of the input object, produced via the final sigmoid activation. The entire flow is guided by solid blue arrows indicating the direction of data propagation.

The figure illustrates the architecture of Focal U-Net, a convolutional neural network designed for image segmentation tasks. The global layout follows a U-shaped structure, consisting of an encoder (left side) and a decoder (right side), connected by skip connections. The input is a grayscale image of size 512×512×1, shown on the far left as a 3D gray block with a sketch-like illustration. The output, on the far right, is also a 512×512×1 image, depicting the segmented result with overlaid red contours indicating detected regions.

The encoder side comprises three downsampling stages. Each stage includes a blue block representing two consecutive 3×3 convolutional layers followed by ReLU activation, and a green block representing a 2×2 max pooling operation. The first stage reduces the spatial dimensions from 512×512 to 256×256 with 64 feature channels. The second stage further reduces to 128×128 with 128 channels. The third stage reduces to 64×64 with 256 channels. These blocks are stacked vertically, decreasing in size and increasing in channel count.

The decoder side mirrors the encoder but performs upsampling. It begins with a large blue block of size 512×512×2, which is the result of the final upsampling step. This block is preceded by three upsampling stages. Each stage includes a red block representing a deconvolution layer, which increases spatial resolution, and a blue block for two 3×3 convolutions with ReLU. The first upsampling stage increases from 64×64 to 128×128 with 128 channels. The second stage increases to 256×256 with 64 channels. The final stage reaches 512×512 with 2 channels. A yellow block labeled 'Argmax' is attached to the last blue block, indicating a final operation to convert the 2-channel output into a single-channel segmentation mask.

Skip connections are represented by dashed blue lines connecting corresponding encoder and decoder stages, allowing feature maps from the encoder to be concatenated with those in the decoder at each level. Solid purple arrows indicate the flow of data through the network, from the encoder to the decoder via these skip connections. The legend at the bottom clarifies the color coding: blue for (3×3 Conv + ReLU) ×2, green for 2×2 Max Pooling, red for Deconv, and yellow for Argmax. The entire structure emphasizes feature reuse and resolution recovery, typical of U-Net architectures, adapted here for focal segmentation.

The figure illustrates the architecture of an adversarial neural network designed for style transfer, specifically for generating colored anime-style images from line art inputs. Following the Feature Extractor is the DR Layer (Dimensionality Reduction Layer), shown as a vertical column of eight green circular nodes enclosed within a thin blue rectangular border. These green circles represent hidden units or neurons in a fully connected layer responsible for reducing the dimensionality of the extracted features. Each green node is connected via dashed black lines to multiple nodes in both the preceding Feature Extractor and the subsequent Binary Optimizer, illustrating a dense, non-local connectivity pattern.

The third and final module is the Binary Optimizer, enclosed in a rounded rectangle with a blue outline similar to the Feature Extractor but smaller in size. The figure illustrates a method for selecting key frames and key segments from a sequence of video frames, using an iterative optimization process based on feature swapping. The global layout is structured horizontally, depicting a pipeline from input frames at the top, through a series of processing stages in the middle, to output selections at the bottom. At the top, a row of eight grayscale video frames shows a tornado-like phenomenon progressing across time. These frames feed into a feature extraction stage labeled '* FC layer', indicating a fully connected layer that processes each frame to extract features.

In the central part of the diagram, three large rounded rectangular modules represent successive iterations of a feature optimization process. Each module contains two dashed circular regions, symbolizing clusters or groups of features. Within these circles, small white circles represent general features, while red circles denote 'key features'—the focus of the optimization. Green solid arrows between features indicate 'Accepted swap', meaning a feature exchange that improves the objective function, while green dashed arrows represent 'Rejected swap', where the exchange is not beneficial. The first module shows initial random assignment of key features, followed by swaps; subsequent modules show the evolution of key features through iterations, with the key features gradually converging to more stable positions. An ellipsis (...) between the second and third modules indicates continuation of this iterative process.

At the bottom, the final output is shown: a row of the same eight video frames, now annotated with colored borders. Red-bordered frames are labeled as 'Key frame', indicating frames containing the most salient key features. Blue-bordered frames are labeled as 'Key segment', representing frames that are part of a continuous segment of interest, likely defined by temporal proximity to key frames. The key features from the final iteration are connected via black lines to their corresponding output frames, showing which frames are selected as key frames or key segments based on the optimized key features.

A legend at the bottom left clarifies the visual elements: a red circle means 'Key feature', a solid green double-headed arrow means 'Accepted swap', and a dashed green double-headed arrow means 'Rejected swap'. Another legend at the bottom right explains the output frame annotations: a red square border denotes 'Key frame', and a blue square border denotes 'Key segment'.

The overall workflow is: input frames → feature extraction via FC layer → initialization of key features → iterative swapping to optimize key features → selection of key frames and key segments based on final key features. This method emphasizes dynamic optimization of feature selection to identify the most representative frames and segments in a video sequence.

The figure presents three distinct operations commonly used in deep learning architectures: spatial convolution, depth-wise convolution, and shift operation, each illustrated in separate panels labeled (a), (b), and (c).

In panel (a), Spatial Convolution, a 3D blue input tensor of dimensions M × D_F × D_F is shown on the left. This tensor is convolved with N filters, each represented as a vertical rectangular prism of size M × D_K × D_K, enclosed within a dashed blue oval. The filters are color-coded (yellow, orange, green, etc.) to distinguish them. The convolution operation is denoted by a multiplication symbol (⊗) between the input and the filter set. The output is a 3D tensor of size N × D_F × D_F, depicted as a stacked block with N layers, where the top layer is yellow, the bottom is green, and intermediate layers are gray, indicating the channel dimension.

Panel (b) illustrates Depth-wise Convolution. The same input tensor (M × D_F × D_F) is shown on the left. Instead of applying N filters simultaneously, this operation applies one filter per input channel. Each filter is a small 3D block of size 1 × D_K × D_K, shown as colored cubes (yellow, orange, green) with a multiplication symbol (⊗) next to each. These filters are applied independently across the M channels of the input, as indicated by the dashed blue oval grouping them. The result is an output tensor of size M × D_F × D_F, visually identical in structure to the input but with updated feature maps, again shown as a stacked block with M layers, top layer yellow, bottom green, and middle gray.

Panel (c) shows the Shift operation. On the left, a 3D tensor of size M × D_F × D_F is depicted with M distinct colored layers (yellow, orange, green). To the right, a shift is applied to each channel, visualized by a 3×3 grid representing a shift matrix with kernel size 3. Each grid has one highlighted cell (lighted) indicating a '1' at that position, while others are '0'. Three such matrices are shown with arrows pointing to the corresponding shifted output: yellow shifts up-right, orange shifts down-left, green shifts down-right. The resulting tensor on the far right shows the shifted positions of the colored layers within the same M × D_F × D_F volume, with dashed lines indicating the original positions before shifting. The shift operation preserves the overall dimensions but rearranges the spatial content within each channel based on the specified shift matrix.

All panels use consistent visual conventions: 3D blocks represent tensors, dimensions are labeled with arrows and variables (M, D_F, D_K, N), and operations are indicated by symbols or directional arrows. The figure uses color coding to differentiate channels and filters, and dashed outlines to group related components. The caption clarifies that in (c), the 3×3 grids denote shift matrices with kernel size 3, where lit cells indicate '1' and white cells indicate '0'.

From these segments, arrows point upward to corresponding rectangular blocks in the 'Spatial Sampling' section: a pink block and a purple block, representing the extracted spatially sampled filters. These blocks then feed into the 'Channel Sampling' section above. Here, each block is expanded vertically into a stack of three rectangles (top, middle, bottom), with the middle rectangle containing vertical dots to indicate repetition. Each worker computes the matrix product of its assigned blocks, resulting in an intermediate product ŜᵢᵀB̃ᵢ, shown as a salmon-colored rectangle next to each worker. These computed results are sent via arrows to the Master node, which is also represented by a computer monitor icon. On the far right, under the label 'output', the result is shown as a salmon-colored rectangle labeled C ≜ AᵀB, enclosed in brackets, indicating the final matrix product. A double-headed arrow (⇒) connects the Master to the output, signifying the decoding step.

The red 'X' on Worker 1's output arrow visually emphasizes the straggler tolerance feature of the framework. The diagram conveys that even if some workers fail or delay, the master can still compute the correct result using a subset of the available results, as per the caption’s explanation.

The figure illustrates the GraphGAN framework, a generative adversarial network approach for graph data. The top portion presents the overall training pipeline: a true data distribution p_true(·|v_c) samples real graph nodes (represented as solid green circles), while a generator G(·|v_c; θ_G) generates synthetic nodes (striped blue circles). These two sets of nodes are fed into a discriminator D, which is trained to distinguish between real and generated samples. The generator is updated via policy gradient, based on feedback from the discriminator, aiming to make G approximate p_true, as indicated by the final output G ≈ p_true. The bottom portion visualizes the progressive improvement of the generator through three stages. In the first stage, labeled 'G underperforms in initial stage', the generator produces mostly incorrect node types (blue striped nodes) compared to the true distribution (green nodes), with only a few correct matches. The central stage, 'G is approaching p_true during adversarial training', shows an intermediate state where the generator's output increasingly resembles the true distribution, with more green nodes appearing among the generated ones. The final stage, 'G is hardly distinguishable from p_true', depicts the converged state where the generated graph structure closely matches the true distribution, with most nodes being correctly classified as green, indicating successful learning. Each graph is centered around a context node v_c (orange circle), connected to other nodes via black edges, representing the local neighborhood structure. The progression is indicated by gray arrows between the three graph states, showing the iterative refinement process.

The figure illustrates the iterative steps of the Online Mirror Descent (OMD) algorithm, structured as a cyclic workflow between two distinct spaces: the Primal and the Dual. The global layout consists of two large polygonal regions placed side-by-side — a salmon-colored hexagon labeled 'Primal' on the left and a light beige octagon labeled 'Dual' on the right. These represent the primal and dual domains, respectively, where the optimization process unfolds. Within the Primal region, two black dots are marked: p(t) at the top and p(t+1) at the bottom, indicating the current and next primal points in the sequence. In the Dual region, two corresponding black dots are shown: ∇F(p(t)) at the top and ∇F(w(t+1)) at the bottom, representing the gradient mappings of the primal points into the dual space.

The visual modules and their attributes are defined by color-coded dashed arrows and labeled mathematical operations. A blue dashed arrow originates from p(t) in the Primal space and points to ∇F(p(t)) in the Dual space, labeled with '∇F(.)', signifying the forward gradient map that transforms the primal point into the dual space. From ∇F(p(t)), a red solid arrow descends to ∇F(w(t+1)) in the Dual space, labeled 'η·g(t)', representing the gradient update step in the dual space, where η is the learning rate and g(t) is the observed gradient at time t. A green dashed arrow then curves from ∇F(w(t+1)) back toward the Primal space, labeled '(∇F)^{-1}(.)', indicating the application of the inverse gradient map to recover the updated primal variable w(t+1). Finally, a purple solid arrow points upward from w(t+1) to p(t+1), labeled implicitly by the caption as the Bregman projection step, which projects the updated point back onto the feasible set (e.g., the simplex) to obtain the next primal iterate.

Connections and arrows form a closed loop: starting from p(t), the algorithm moves to the dual space via the gradient map (blue), performs an update (red), returns to the primal space via the inverse gradient map (green), and applies a projection to enforce constraints (purple), yielding p(t+1). This cycle captures the essence of OMD: leveraging a non-Euclidean geometry through a mirror map F, enabling efficient updates in the dual space while maintaining feasibility in the primal. The figure’s design emphasizes the separation of primal and dual spaces and the role of the gradient map and its inverse in bridging them, with the projection step ensuring convergence within the constraint set.

The figure illustrates a deep learning framework for training a convolutional neural network (CNN) to optimize correlation-based object tracking or detection. The global layout is left-to-right, depicting a data flow from raw input images through a fully convolutional network to a correlation computation stage, followed by a loss calculation and feedback loop for training.

On the far left, two raw image patches labeled x_raw and y_raw are shown as tilted rectangular images with dashed lines converging toward a central gray 3D cube labeled 'Fully Conv. Layers'. These represent input image pairs differing in object appearance or spatial translation. The cube symbolizes the fully convolutional network, which processes both inputs simultaneously and outputs feature representations x_θ and y_θ, indicated by white boxes with black borders connected via curved green arrows.

From x_θ, a solid dark blue arrow leads to a circular symbol with an asterisk (*), representing circular cross-correlation. The output of this operation is a grayscale heatmap labeled 'Correlation plane: g^c', showing a bright peak at the center, indicating a strong match. Below this, a downward arrow connects to a loss function expression: L = ||g^c - g||², which measures the squared difference between the computed correlation plane g^c and a desired target plane g.

The desired plane g is depicted as a black square with a bright circular spot at the center, labeled 'Desired plane: g'. An upward arrow from g points to the loss term, emphasizing that the loss is computed relative to this target. Another arrow from the loss term points back to the correlation operator, indicating that gradients are propagated backward to update the model.

In parallel, the output y_θ feeds into a gray rectangular box containing a mathematical formula: h_θ^l = ℱ^{-1} { G^* ⊙ Y_θ^l / (∑_{m=1}^d Y_θ^m ⊙ Y_θ^{m*} + λ) }, which represents the computation of a correlation filter h_θ using the Fourier domain. This filter is then passed via a large gray arrow to a white box labeled h_θ, which connects to the correlation operator via a thick dark blue arrow, indicating that h_θ is used as the filter in the correlation step.

The overall workflow shows that the CNN learns parameters θ such that when the learned filter h_θ is applied to the feature map x_θ, the resulting correlation plane g^c closely matches the desired response g, minimizing the loss L. The diagram emphasizes end-to-end training where the CNN features and the correlation filter are jointly optimized.

The figure illustrates an architectural framework for an NMT (Neural Machine Translation) decoder enhanced with a phrase memory mechanism, designed to integrate both word-level and phrase-level generation strategies. The final decoding step is connected via a dashed arrow to a decision point marked in red text: 'word or phrase ?', symbolizing the choice between generating a word or a phrase at that position.

This decision is managed by a beige rectangular box labeled 'Balancer', positioned centrally. The Balancer receives inputs from both the Phrase generator and the Word generator (another white rectangular box below it), and uses a weighting parameter λ to control the contribution of each path. Specifically, a solid arrow from the Balancer to the Phrase generator is annotated with 'w = λ', while a solid arrow from the Balancer to the Word generator is annotated with 'w = 1 - λ', indicating that the Balancer dynamically adjusts the weight between phrase-based and word-based generation.

A dashed arrow from the Balancer loops back to the NMT decoder’s final step, suggesting feedback or influence on the decoding decision. Additionally, a solid arrow connects the NMT decoder directly to the Word generator, showing that the decoder can also feed into the word-level generation path independently.

The overall structure emphasizes a hybrid approach where the NMT decoder leverages both neural and statistical (SMT-derived) components through the phrase memory and balancer, enabling flexible switching between word and phrase generation modes during translation.

The figure illustrates the architecture of a non-local filtering layer, structured as a two-branch pipeline that converges into a collaborative filtering operation. A black arrow connects the Convolution Layer to this Collaborative Filtering Layer.

The bottom branch starts with the Block Matching Layer, shown as a rectangular box containing a blue square labeled 'R' connected by black arrows to three smaller, light gray squares arranged below it, representing matched blocks. The final output of the entire structure proceeds from the Collaborative Filtering Layer to the right, indicated by a black arrow exiting the box. The overall design emphasizes the integration of local feature extraction (via convolution) and non-local context aggregation (via block matching and collaborative filtering) to compute a refined output.

The figure presents a schematic illustration of an actor-critic based captioning model, designed for generating sequential outputs such as image captions. The central and right portion of the diagram shows a vertical stack of three rows of blocks, forming the core of the actor-critic architecture. The top row consists of a sequence of colored blocks (light purple, light blue, light green, pink, sky blue, lime green, black) representing the action space or output tokens at each time step. Above this row, the equation a_{t+1} ~ π_θ(s_t) indicates that the next action (token) is sampled from a policy distribution parameterized by θ, conditioned on the current state s_t. The bottom row contains a sequence of colored blocks (light peach, orange, dark orange, brown, light peach) labeled V^π(s_t), denoting the value function estimated by the critic network for the current state under policy π.

The connections between these rows are shown via vertical arrows: upward arrows from the RNN cells to the action row indicate the generation of actions, while downward arrows from the RNN cells to the value row indicate the computation of state values. A legend on the right clarifies the color coding: a red block denotes the start token a_0, a black block denotes the end token a_T, and a gray block denotes an RNN cell. The start token is positioned at the beginning of the action sequence, and the end token marks its termination, indicating that the model generates sequences until the end token is produced. The entire architecture operates in a sequential manner, where the RNN processes the state representation from the encoder and generates a sequence of tokens while simultaneously estimating the value of each state to guide the policy learning process.

The figure illustrates the architecture of a spectral-invariant feature descriptor H, constructed from weighted histograms derived from multi-scale gradient maps. These maps feed into corresponding histogram computations: the top group generates h₁ (magnitude histograms), the middle group generates h₃ (O-HOG histograms), and the bottom group generates h₂ (direction histograms). Each histogram is represented as a horizontal bar chart with multiple colored bars (yellow, green, orange, blue) inside dashed rectangular bins, arranged sequentially along an axis.

From these histograms, three dashed arrows—colored red for h₁, pink for h₃, and blue for h₂—converge toward two large 3D tensor structures on the right, labeled H_p and H_q. These tensors are depicted as transparent rectangular prisms with internal dashed lines indicating layered structure. H_p is shown in greenish-blue, and H_q in orange-gray. Both tensors receive inputs via solid black arrows from the respective histograms. Inside each tensor, diagonal cross-sections (green and purple lines) illustrate internal processing or slicing operations.

Below the tensors, a summation expression h^(i) + ... + h^(j) + ... indicates the aggregation of individual histogram contributions across scales or regions. This sum feeds into a final black box labeled 'BWNCC', which stands for Binary Weighted Normalized Cross-Correlation, suggesting the final matching or similarity computation step.

The overall workflow proceeds from multi-scale gradient map analysis through weighted histogram extraction, followed by tensor-based aggregation into H_p and H_q, and culminates in a BWNCC operation for feature comparison. The figure emphasizes the hierarchical and multi-channel nature of the descriptor construction, with clear visual differentiation between magnitude and direction components and their respective histogram representations.

The figure illustrates the framework of the self-supervised body part regressor (SSBR), designed for learning representations from medical imaging volumes without explicit supervision. The global layout is left-to-right, depicting a data processing pipeline starting from raw 3D volumetric input on the left, progressing through feature extraction and scoring, and ending with loss computation and backpropagation on the right.

On the far left, a gray 3D cube labeled 'Volume i' represents a 3D medical image volume. From this volume, three axial slices—labeled 'Slice j', 'Slice j+k', and 'Slice j+2k'—are randomly selected, as indicated by the text 'Randomly pick i, j, k'. Each slice is shown as a grayscale axial CT scan image with a blue rectangular crop highlighting a region of interest. These slices are further processed by extracting 'Random 2D crops', which are then grouped into a 'Minibatch' for input into the network.

The minibatch feeds into a blue trapezoidal module labeled 'VGG-16 Conv1 - Conv5', representing the first five convolutional blocks of the VGG-16 architecture. This module extracts deep features from the input crops. The output of this module connects to a vertical stack of four rectangular layers forming a feature processing head: the bottom layer is blue and labeled 'Conv6 (1x1,512,1)', followed by a teal layer labeled 'ReLU6', then a green layer labeled 'Global avg. pool.', and finally a mustard-yellow layer labeled 'Fc7 (512x1)'. These layers progressively reduce spatial dimensions and produce a fixed-length feature vector.

From the Fc7 layer, an upward arrow leads to a label 'Slice scores: s₁, s₂, s₃, ...', indicating that each input slice is assigned a scalar score. These scores are used to compute two types of losses, shown as orange rectangles: 'Order loss' enforces the constraint s₁ < s₂ < s₃ < ..., ensuring scores increase monotonically with slice depth; 'Distance loss' enforces s₂−s₁ = s₃−s₂ = ..., ensuring uniform spacing between consecutive scores. Both losses are connected via arrows to a large blue curved arrow labeled 'Backprop', which loops back to the VGG-16 module, indicating that gradients are propagated backward through the network to update weights during training.

The diagram uses consistent visual attributes: gray cubes for 3D volumes, black-and-white images for slices, blue rectangles for crops and network modules, colored layers for the feature head, and orange boxes for loss functions. Text labels are placed adjacent to or within components to clarify function. The flow is directed by solid blue arrows, clearly delineating the forward pass and backpropagation path.

The global layout is divided into two main training pathways and a central testing phase, arranged horizontally. On the left, a set of transformed unlabeled face images is grouped under a red curly brace labeled 'Transformed unlabeled data', with the notation T_G below it, indicating the application of a transformation group G. These images show variations such as different angles, lighting, or expressions, suggesting the presence of nuisance transformations. A thick blue arrow points downward from this group to a beige rectangular box labeled 'MMIF(x)', which represents the proposed MMIF model. Below this box, the text 'invariant to G' indicates that the model learns features robust to the specified transformations.

On the right side, a set of non-transformed labeled face images is grouped under a blue curly brace labeled 'Non-transformed labeled data', followed by the mathematical symbol x. This set includes diverse faces, and a green vertical arrow labeled 'Train' points from it to a gray rectangular box labeled 'F(x)', representing a traditional classifier. Below this box, the text 'not invariant to G' highlights that this model does not inherently learn invariance to the transformation group G.

In the center, a test image x, depicted as a grayscale face wearing glasses, is shown. Two orange bidirectional arrows connect this test image to both the MMIF(x) and F(x) models, indicating that the same test input is processed by both systems for comparison. Additionally, another green 'Train' arrow descends from the non-transformed labeled data to the F(x) model, emphasizing that the traditional classifier is trained solely on labeled data without explicit exposure to transformed examples.

The visual modules are distinct: the MMIF(x) box is beige, while F(x) is gray, visually differentiating the two approaches. The transformation group G is denoted by a script G, and the training process is indicated by green arrows. The connections between components are color-coded: blue for the flow from transformed unlabeled data to MMIF, green for training the traditional classifier, and orange for the test phase. The figure effectively contrasts the two methods: MMIF leverages both labeled and unlabeled (transformed) data to learn invariance, whereas F(x) relies only on labeled data and thus lacks such invariance. The caption reinforces that MMIF solves the Unlabeled Transformation Problem by incorporating invariance learned from unlabeled data undergoing the nuisance transformation.

The figure illustrates a modular neural network architecture designed for predicting Q-values from raw pixel inputs, consisting of two main components: a Perception Module and a Control Module, connected via a Bottleneck layer. The overall layout is left-to-right, with input on the far left, processing stages in the center, and loss computation on the right.

[1] Global Layout and Structure:
The diagram is horizontally structured into three primary sections: the Perception Module (left), the Bottleneck (center), and the Control Module (right). Inputs are shown at the far left, feeding into the Perception Module. Outputs from the Bottleneck feed into the Control Module, which produces Q-values. Two loss functions—Perception Loss (L_p) and Task Loss (L_q)—are computed from intermediate and final outputs, respectively, and are visually linked back to the network for training purposes.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes:
The Perception Module is enclosed in a light beige box and labeled accordingly. It receives either a simulated 84×84 grayscale image (top) or a real-world robot image (bottom), both labeled 'I'. This module comprises three convolutional layers: Conv1 uses a 7×7 convolution with stride 2, followed by ReLU activation and 64 filters; Conv2 uses a 4×4 convolution with stride 2, ReLU, and 64 filters; Conv3 uses a 3×3 convolution with stride 1, ReLU, and 64 filters. Each convolutional layer is represented as a light purple 3D rectangular prism with labeled filter count.

Following the Perception Module is the Bottleneck, depicted as a tall purple rectangle labeled 'BN'. Inside it is a green rectangle labeled '5 units', representing a fully connected layer that outputs the latent representation Θ. The caption notes that Θ’s values are normalized to [0,1].

The Control Module is enclosed in a light blue box and contains three fully connected layers: FC_c1 (400 units), FC_c2 (300 units), and FC_c3 (9 units), each represented as a vertical green rectangle. Each layer includes ReLU activation and is labeled 'fully conn.' above it. The final output layer (FC_c3) is explicitly labeled 'Q-values'.

Loss components are shown as colored boxes: Perception Loss (L_p) is in a light green box at the top right, connected to the Bottleneck output. Task Loss (L_q) is in a salmon-pink box on the far right, connected to the Q-values output. The Bottleneck also has a label L_q^BN indicating a specific loss component associated with it.

[3] Connections and Arrows:
Black arrows indicate forward propagation: from input I to Conv1, then sequentially through Conv2 and Conv3, followed by a fully connected layer leading to the Bottleneck. From the Bottleneck, a black arrow points to FC_c1, which connects to FC_c2, then to FC_c3, producing Q-values.

Blue lines represent loss feedback: one from the Bottleneck to the Perception Loss (L_p) box, and another from the Q-values output to the Task Loss (L_q) box. These indicate that the network is trained using a combination of these losses, with the Perception Loss applied to the bottleneck features and the Task Loss applied to the final Q-values.

On the right side, the 'Image Transformation Network' is enclosed in a dashed rectangle and consists of multiple stacked white rectangular blocks representing convolutional layers. This network receives input from the 'Content Image' via a blue arrow and also incorporates learned filters derived from the 'Style Image'. Specifically, the style features extracted from the Style Image through VGG-16 are passed through two fully connected layers labeled 'hidden filters', represented as vertical columns of circles with ellipses indicating intermediate dimensions. The final output, 'Transferred Image', is produced at the bottom of the transformation network and is linked back to the VGG-16 for loss computation, forming a closed-loop optimization process. The overall workflow involves optimizing the transformation network to minimize both content and style losses, thereby generating an image that preserves the content of the input content image while adopting the artistic style of the style image.

The figure presents a data flow graph illustrating the ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers) optimization process for a general compressed sensing MRI (CS-MRI) model. The overall layout is horizontal, progressing from left to right, depicting the sequential stages of reconstruction from undersampled k-space data to the final reconstructed MR image. On the far left, a black-and-white image labeled 'Sampling data in k-space' shows a radial pattern of sampled points in k-space, representing the input to the reconstruction pipeline. This input feeds into a sequence of computational nodes arranged in a linear chain with intermediate feedback loops, culminating on the far right in a grayscale brain MR image labeled 'Reconstructed MR image'.

The core structure consists of three types of nodes, each represented by a light beige rectangular box with a dark blue border: reconstruction variables (denoted as X^(n)), denoising variables (Z^(n)), and multiplier variables (M^(n)). These nodes are organized in a staged progression, where each stage n involves a set of operations: X^(n) is updated based on previous state X^(n-1) and multiplier M^(n-1), then Z^(n) is derived from X^(n), and finally M^(n) is updated using both X^(n) and Z^(n). This entire process is encapsulated within a dashed orange rectangle labeled 'stage n', indicating the iterative nature of the algorithm.

The connections between nodes are represented by thick dark blue arrows, indicating the direction of data flow. From the initial k-space data, a single arrow leads to X^(1), followed by a series of dots indicating intermediate steps, leading to X^(n-1). From X^(n-1), two arrows branch out: one to Z^(n-1) and another to M^(n-1). M^(n-1) then feeds into M^(n) via a direct arrow, and also connects to X^(n) and Z^(n) through additional arrows, reflecting the coupling in the ADMM framework. Within stage n, X^(n) receives input from X^(n-1) and M^(n-1), produces Z^(n), which in turn contributes to updating M^(n). M^(n) then feeds forward to M^(n+1) and also influences X^(n+1) and Z^(n+1). This pattern repeats across stages until the final X^(Ns+1) is produced, which outputs to the reconstructed MR image.

The figure emphasizes the iterative refinement process, where each stage refines the reconstruction by alternating between updating the image estimate (X), applying a denoising step (Z), and updating the Lagrange multipliers (M). The visual design uses consistent node shapes and colors to distinguish variable types, while the directional arrows clearly map the dependencies and information flow. The caption clarifies that this graph serves as the foundation for defining deep ADMM-Nets, where neural networks may replace or enhance the traditional operations within each stage.

The figure presents a two-part architectural diagram of the SchNet model, divided by a vertical dashed line into a global overview on the left and a detailed breakdown of the interaction block on the right. Inside the block, the atomic features are processed through a series of layers: first an 'atom-wise, 256' layer, followed by a 'cfconv, 256' layer (continuous filter convolution), then another 'atom-wise, 256' layer, a 'shifted softplus' activation function, and finally another 'atom-wise, 256' layer. The output of the final atom-wise layer is summed with the original input features (x'₁, ..., x'ₙ) via a circular '+' node, producing the updated atomic features (v'₁, ..., v'ₙ). This updated feature vector is then passed to the next interaction block or serves as the final output (x'^(l+1)₁, ..., x'^(l+1)ₙ). The shifted softplus activation function is defined as ssp(x) = ln(0.5e^x + 0.5), as noted in the caption. All layers are parameterized with 256 neurons, as indicated in their labels. The figure presents two diagrams illustrating the structure and implementation of a ResNet building block, labeled as (a) and (b), respectively. The global layout is split into two vertical columns: the left column (a) shows a simplified, abstract representation of the information flow, while the right column (b) provides a detailed, layered implementation as described in the original ResNet paper. Both diagrams share the same core concept: a residual connection that adds the input directly to the output of a transformation function, enabling deeper networks by mitigating vanishing gradients.

In diagram (a), the structure begins with an input x entering a 'weight layer' (represented as a black-bordered rectangle with white fill). This is followed by a ReLU activation (labeled 'ReLU' next to the arrow), then another 'weight layer'. The outputs of these two layers are combined via an element-wise addition operation, denoted by a circular '+' symbol. A skip connection, represented by a curved arrow, bypasses the two weight layers and directly connects the input x to the addition node. The final output is labeled y = F(x) + id(x), where F(x) represents the transformation through the two weight layers and ReLU, and id(x) is the identity mapping (the direct input). The entire transformation path is labeled F(x), and the identity path is labeled id(x).

Diagram (b) expands on this with more specific neural network operations. It starts with an 'Input x' box at the top. The main transformation path F(x) consists of five sequential layers: a blue 'Convolution' layer, a green 'Batch Norm' layer, a red 'ReLU' layer, another blue 'Convolution' layer, and a final green 'Batch Norm' layer. These layers are stacked vertically, each connected by downward arrows. The identity path id(x) is shown as a curved arrow from the 'Input x' box directly to the addition node. The outputs of both paths converge at a white rectangular box containing a '+' symbol, representing element-wise addition. Following this, a red 'ReLU' layer processes the summed result, leading to the 'Output y' box. The equation y = F(x) + id(x) is written below the output, consistent with diagram (a). The color coding is consistent: blue for convolutional layers, green for batch normalization, and red for ReLU activations. All boxes are rectangular with black borders, and connections are solid black arrows indicating data flow direction. The figure caption clarifies that the circular '+' symbol denotes element-wise addition, and references the original ResNet paper.

The figure illustrates the Higher-order Siamese-GCN framework, a method for graph similarity learning using a siamese network architecture with shared weights. The global layout is divided into four main stages arranged horizontally: Input graphs (leftmost), Random walk augmented input graphs, Siamese Network, and Similarity Learning (rightmost). Each stage is enclosed in a dashed rectangular box with a descriptive title.

In the first stage, two separate input graphs are shown, labeled (G₁,y₁) and (G₂,y₂), each represented as an undirected graph with nodes of different colors (red, blue, green, orange, purple, gray) connected by black edges. These graphs serve as the initial inputs.

The second stage shows the same two graphs after undergoing a random walk process, indicated by dashed blue lines connecting nodes that were not originally linked. This augmentation creates higher-order structural information, resulting in a combined representation (G₁,G₂,y) for both graphs, which are then fed into the next stage.

The third stage is the Siamese Network, consisting of two identical Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), labeled 'Graph Convolutional Network I' and 'Graph Convolutional Network II'. Each GCN is depicted as a sequence of blue 3D blocks representing convolutional layers, with ellipses indicating multiple layers. A bidirectional arrow labeled 'Shared weights' connects the two networks, emphasizing that they share the same parameters during training.

The outputs from both GCNs are then passed to the fourth stage, Similarity Learning. Here, the two feature vectors are combined via a dot product operation, symbolized by a circular node with a multiplication sign (×). The result is fed into a fully connected (FC) layer, represented as a single blue 3D block, which produces the final similarity score S. A dashed line from the FC layer points to the label 'Similarity score', indicating the output of the entire framework.

All connections between stages are shown with solid black arrows, while the random walk augmentation within the second stage uses dashed blue lines. The overall flow is left-to-right, depicting a pipeline from raw graph inputs to a learned similarity score through deep graph representation learning.

The figure presents two distinct attention mechanisms for context aggregation in feature maps, labeled as (a) Non-local block and (b) Criss-Cross Attention block, arranged vertically with a horizontal gradient bar at the bottom indicating a progression from 'Few context' to 'Rich context'.

In part (a), the Non-local block begins with an input feature map represented as a grid of light gray squares, where one cell is highlighted in blue to denote the current query position. This input is processed through two parallel pathways: one generates a dense attention map of size H×W, depicted as a grid filled with varying shades of green (darker green indicating higher attention weights), while the other pathway produces a plain light gray grid representing the value features. These two outputs converge at a circular node marked with a multiplication symbol (⊗), signifying element-wise multiplication or weighted summation. The result is an output feature map of the same spatial dimensions, shown as a grid of dark gray squares with one cell highlighted in red, indicating the aggregated feature at the corresponding position.

Part (b) illustrates the Criss-Cross Attention block, which operates in two sequential stages. The first stage starts with the same input grid with a blue-highlighted query position. It computes a sparse attention map of size H+W−1, shown as a cross-shaped pattern of green cells centered on the query, with darker green indicating stronger attention. This sparse map is multiplied (via ⊗) with a value feature grid (light gray) to produce an intermediate output, where the corresponding position is highlighted in yellow. This intermediate output then serves as the input to the second stage, which repeats the same process: generating another sparse attention map (H+W−1) and multiplying it with a new value grid to yield the final output feature map, again with one cell highlighted in red. The entire process demonstrates a recurrent structure that allows each position to gather contextual information from all pixels across iterations.

Both diagrams use grids to represent feature maps, with color coding to indicate query positions (blue), attention weights (green gradients), intermediate results (yellow), and final outputs (red). The connections between modules are shown as solid black arrows, indicating the flow of data. The figure emphasizes that the Criss-Cross Attention block achieves rich context aggregation with significantly fewer parameters (about 2√N weights) compared to the Non-local block's dense N weights, while both ultimately enable global context capture. Residual connections are omitted for clarity.

The figure presents the architectural overview of the Adapnet++ model, a deep learning framework for semantic segmentation. The second stage involves the 'eASPP' (efficient atrous spatial pyramid pooling) module, shown as a grid of small green squares arranged in a 4x4 pattern with additional green squares branching off, indicating parallel processing paths for capturing multi-scale contextual information. The final output is a 'Segmented Prediction', visualized as a color-coded image with distinct regions, representing the pixel-wise classification result. All connections between modules are shown as solid black arrows, indicating the flow of data through the network. The diagram emphasizes the hierarchical processing and integration of multi-scale features through skip connections to achieve accurate semantic segmentation.

The figure illustrates the architectural design of a residual block, commonly used in deep neural networks to address the vanishing gradient problem and enable training of very deep networks. The global layout is horizontal, depicting a left-to-right data flow through two sequential layers followed by a shortcut connection that skips these layers. The structure begins with an input labeled 'x', represented by a gray arrow pointing into the first blue rectangular module. This module symbolizes a neural network layer, composed of multiple yellow circular nodes arranged vertically, indicating neurons or feature maps. A gray arrow connects this first module to a second identical blue rectangular module, representing the next layer in the sequence. The output of the second module is labeled 'F(x)', indicating the transformation applied by the two layers to the input x. From the input 'x', a curved black line labeled 'x - Identity' bypasses the two layers and directly connects to a circular node containing a blue plus sign, which represents element-wise addition. This shortcut connection allows the original input to be added to the transformed output F(x), producing the final output labeled 'F(x) + x'. The visual modules are characterized by their distinct shapes and colors: the layers are tall blue rectangles with yellow circles inside, while the addition operation is a small circle with a blue '+' symbol. All arrows are gray and point rightward, indicating forward propagation. The connections include both the direct forward path through the layers and the identity shortcut path, which is explicitly labeled to emphasize its role in residual learning. The figure effectively conveys the core idea that the network learns the residual function F(x) = H(x) - x, where H(x) is the desired underlying mapping, allowing for easier optimization by adding the identity mapping directly to the learned residual.

The figure illustrates the reverse cycle of a cycle-consistent Variational Autoencoder (VAE) architecture, designed to ensure consistency between latent representations across different data sources. The global layout is horizontally structured into two parallel processing streams, one for each input source, labeled X₁ (green square) and X₂ (red square), which are indicated as being randomly sampled. Each stream follows an identical encoding-decoding pipeline: first, the input X₁ or X₂ passes through a blue trapezoidal 'Enc' (encoder) module, producing two outputs — a latent code Z₁ or Z₂ (black arrows pointing rightward) and a style vector S₁ or S₂ (black arrows pointing upward). These style vectors are passed directly to the corresponding decoder. The latent codes Z₁ and Z₂ are then combined with a shared latent variable Zi, drawn from a standard normal distribution N(0, I), represented by a gray oval with a black dot labeled Zi. This combination feeds into a shared blue trapezoidal 'Dec' (decoder) module, which generates two reconstructed images, X''₁ (green square) and X''₂ (red square), corresponding to the original inputs. The reconstructed images are then fed into separate 'Enc' modules again, producing new latent codes Z''₁ and Z''₂, which are shown converging toward the original Zi, indicating the cycle-consistency constraint. The style vectors S₁ and S₂ are also passed forward from the first encoder to the second encoder in each branch, maintaining style information throughout the cycle. The visual modules consist of colored squares for inputs and reconstructions (green for X₁/X''₁, red for X₂/X''₂), blue trapezoids for encoder and decoder blocks, and a gray oval for the latent space. All connections are represented by solid black arrows, with labels indicating the flow of data (Z₁, Z₂, S₁, S₂, Z''₁, Z''₂, Zi). The diagram emphasizes that after reconstruction and re-encoding, the latent codes Z''₁ and Z''₂ should converge to the original sampled point Zi, validating the cycle-consistency property of the model.

The figure illustrates a multi-stage Saak transform-based method designed to filter adversarial perturbations from input data before classification by a CNN. The global layout is a left-to-right pipeline, starting with 'Adversarial Examples' on the far left and ending with 'Predictions' on the far right, with intermediate processing stages in between. The process begins with a blue rectangular block labeled 'Adversarial Examples', representing the input data containing adversarial noise. This input is processed through a forward Saak transform, depicted as a blue cube with a small black dot, symbolizing the transformation into frequency components. The output of this step is split into two parts: a blue rectangular block labeled 'low frequency' and a gray rectangular block labeled 'high frequency', indicating the separation of signal components. The high-frequency component, which typically contains adversarial perturbations, is then passed through a filtering stage represented by a gray block labeled 'Saak coefficients Filtering'.
